title: The laugh in Maya's hall
hook: Duryodhana is fooled by Maya's hall and laughed at, and a host's duty to a guest is broken
carry: atithi devo bhava: the guest is god

segments.voice: Yesterday a light rose from Shishupala and entered Krishna, and the Rajasuya was finished: what the mind dwells on, it reaches.

The guests have gone home, but one has stayed behind. Duryodhana lingers at Indraprastha with his uncle Shakuni, wandering through the great hall the asura builder Maya made for the Pandavas. It's a hall of wonders, and wonders can be tricky. Floors that look like water. Water that looks like floor. Doors that seem open and aren't. A new story starts here, the dice game. But it doesn't start with dice. It starts with a man walking through a beautiful room and getting it wrong, again and again.
screen: `ONE GUEST STAYS BEHIND.` → `MAYA'S HALL OF WONDERS.` → `IT STARTS WITHOUT DICE.`

segments.voice: In the telling, Duryodhana comes to a spot on the floor that looks like a pool. It's crystal, but he takes it for water and gathers up his clothes to wade across. Nothing wet. Then he comes to a real pool, so clear it looks like solid floor, and walks straight in, clothes and all. Bhima sees it, and laughs. The servants laugh too. Yudhishthira, the host, sends him dry clothes. By the end, the hall has fooled him over and over, and his mistakes have had an audience. Now, the teaching. Hindu homes keep an old line, from the Taittiriya Upanishad: atithi devo bhava, let the guest be a god to you. That's why so many families meet a visitor with water, a seat, and far too much food. In Maya's hall the line is tested. Yudhishthira keeps it: his guest is soaked, so he covers him. Bhima forgets it: his guest is soaked, so he laughs. Many teachers read the moment this way: the dice game, and the war after it, open from a guest shamed in the house that should have sheltered him. The poem doesn't excuse what Duryodhana does next. It shows where the wound opened. Today it's the same small test. Someone at your table spills, mispronounces a dish, walks into the wrong room. Yudhishthira's way is to hand them the dry clothes before anyone gets to laugh.
screen: `CRYSTAL TAKEN FOR WATER.` · `A POOL TAKEN FOR FLOOR.` · `BHIMA LAUGHS. YUDHISHTHIRA SENDS CLOTHES.` · `ATITHI DEVO BHAVA: THE GUEST IS A GOD.` · then, large: `THE WOUND OPENS BEFORE THE DICE.`

segments.voice: Picture someone coming to your door this week: a friend, a neighbor, someone you don't know well. In your mind, do what Hindu homes have done for centuries: open the door, offer a glass of water, offer a seat, and let them feel like the most important person in the room. Then remember one time a guest of yours was embarrassed, and see yourself handing them the dry clothes. If you pray, you can bring that guest into your prayer; if not, simply wish them ease.
Dyuta, the game of dice this story is named for. A story that doesn't begin with dice, but with a guest fooled by Maya's hall, and laughed at as he falls.
Your line: atithi devo bhava, the guest is god. Yudhishthira sent dry clothes; Bhima laughed. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindu homes still greet a guest with water, a seat and food, following atithi devo bhava; and some storytellers treat Duryodhana's humiliation in Maya's hall as the opening of the dice-game story.

fork.setup: you're the host. a guest in your house, one who has never wished you well, has just walked into your pool in full royal dress. what does atithi devo bhava ask of you?
options: cover him: send dry clothes, and let no one laugh.
fork.reveal: the guest is a god in your house, even a difficult one. Yudhishthira sent dry clothes; Bhima laughed, and many teachers read that laugh as where the quarrel began.

original.note: Sanskrit dyūta: dice play, gambling; the name of the section of the poem this story begins.

trapdoor: what you thought: the dice game is about luck.
what it means: it grows from a guest shamed in his cousin's hall, where the host's duty, atithi devo bhava, was kept by Yudhishthira and broken by Bhima's laugh.
what a scholar hears: the poem opens the dice story with a scene of mistaken appearances, and the game itself will turn on things not being what they seem.
recall: gods cursed to be born as men

chat.meaning: Bhima laughed when his guest fell into the pool in Maya's hall, and the quarrel began there. Hindu homes keep atithi devo bhava: the guest is a god, so you cover them, never laugh.

Maya.meaning: the asura builder who made the Pandavas' hall

asura.meaning: a powerful being of the old stories, often opposed to the gods

Shakuni.meaning: Duryodhana's uncle, a master at dice

Indraprastha.meaning: the Pandavas' city, where the Rajasuya is held

Dyuta.meaning: a game of dice, played for stakes

atithi.meaning: a guest; in atithi devo bhava, 'let the guest be a god to you'

sources.ref: Mahabharata, Sabha Parva, Dyuta Parva (Duryodhana in Maya's hall: crystal taken for water, the pool, Bhima's laughter, the doors)
Taittiriya Upanishad 1.11.2 (atithi devo bhava, 'let the guest be a god to you', among the teacher's parting instructions)

notes: All paraphrase. Confirm the sequence in Ganguli: crystal mistaken for water, the clear pool he falls into, Bhima and the servants laughing, Yudhishthira sending clothes, the closed and open doors.

Popular retellings add Draupadi laughing and a taunt about the blind king's son; this script leaves that out. A Keeper should check what Ganguli's text says about who laughed before any later day mentions Draupadi here.
The original note says Dyuta is the name of the section; confirm (Ganguli titles it Dyuta Parva).
The trapdoor's third floor is an interpretive reading of theme, not a textual claim; a Keeper may prefer a plainer line.
